description: Project Proteus consists of a team of dedicated students working towards the health and safety of astronauts
summary: Space exploration is about more than reaching new worlds; it is also about protecting the people who make it possible. Project Proteus is our team's effort to address five major challenges of human spaceflight through five dedicated, research-driven applications, brought together under one platform. From radiation and microgravity to pressure-related physiological changes, isolation and hostile habitat environments, each application explores a different aspect of astronaut safety. Our vision is to bring these solutions together into a unified, intelligent system that helps us better understand, monitor and address the risks of living and working beyond Earth.
details:
THE IDEA BEHIND PROTEUS

Human spaceflight presents challenges that go far beyond engineering a spacecraft capable of reaching its destination. Every astronaut must live and work in an environment that is fundamentally different from Earth, where radiation, altered gravity, physiological changes, isolation and the conditions inside a closed habitat can all affect human health and mission performance.

We began Project Proteus with a simple question: How can technology help us better understand and address the different risks that astronauts face during space exploration?

Rather than approaching these challenges as one broad problem, our team decided to investigate five major areas of human-spaceflight safety and develop a dedicated application for each. The result is Project Proteus: a unified platform bringing together five specialised, research-driven solutions under one mission.

FIVE CHALLENGES. FIVE DEDICATED SOLUTIONS.

01. MUTATION-MAP — Adressing Space Radiation

Space radiation can affect the human body at a cellular and molecular level. Mutation-MAP explores a research-based approach to understanding this risk by bringing together personal radiation dosimetry, biological measurements and individual baselines. Its proposed monitoring framework aims to connect exposure history with biological response, making it easier to examine changes over time rather than relying on radiation exposure figures alone.

02. AEROLOAD SENTINEL — Addressing the Effects of Microgravity

The absence of Earth's gravity gradually changes the mechanical demands placed on the human body. AeroLoad Sentinel focuses on the musculoskeletal and sensorimotor challenges associated with microgravity, exploring ways to monitor bone-loading context, muscle function, balance adaptation and related physiological trends. Its central approach follows a Detect–Warn–Prescribe–Verify framework, with the aim of supporting more informed monitoring and countermeasure planning.

03. AEROFLUX — Adressing Space-Related Pressure and Fluid Shifts

Microgravity changes the normal pressure gradients within the human body and contributes to the redistribution of bodily fluids. AeroFlux explores a wearable, multi-chamber lower-body pressure concept designed to investigate how controlled pressure differences might help address some of these changes. The concept combines physiological monitoring with a proposed pressure-based countermeasure approach, while recognising the need for further engineering and scientific validation.

04. ISOLATION & CONFINEMENT — Supporting Human Performance

Long-duration missions place astronauts in confined environments with demanding schedules, restricted social interaction and disrupted day-night cues. Our isolation and confinement solution explores sleep-opportunity tracking, circadian monitoring, cognitive-performance trends, adaptive lighting and work-rest scheduling. Its purpose is to support awareness of changes in human readiness and help mission teams better understand the effects of prolonged isolation.

05. HOSTILE CLOSED ENVIRONMENTS — Monitoring the Space Habitat

A spacecraft is a closed environment where even small changes in atmospheric and environmental conditions can matter. This solution focuses on monitoring and interpreting potential habitat risks, including carbon dioxide levels, acoustic exposure, chemical contaminants, airborne particulates and microbial environmental data. It brings together different environmental monitoring approaches to support a clearer understanding of the conditions in which astronauts live and work.

ONE PLATFORM, A CONNECTED MISSION VISION

Although each application addresses a different hazard, we believe their greatest value lies in bringing them together.

Proteus is designed around the idea of a shared mission picture, where hazard-specific information can be explored within a consistent platform. Its proposed common architecture connects mission timelines, personal baselines, sensor and research data, and evidence-based interpretation.

The intended workflow is straight forward: capture relevant information, check its quality and source, interpret it using appropriate baselines and models, communicate meaningful findings, and leave important decisions to the relevant human experts.

This matters because astronaut safety cannot be understood through a single measurement or isolated system. A more complete picture requires us to consider the human body, the spacecraft environment and the conditions of the mission together.

THE RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BEHIND OUR WORK

A significant part of our effort has gone into understanding the science behind the problems we are trying to address. We have worked through individual research areas for all five hazards, examining NASA resources, publicly available research datasets, scientific publications and relevant technical standards.

This research has helped shape the design and direction of each application, from radiation dosimetry and biological response to microgravity-related physiological changes, pressure-based concepts, cognitive readiness and habitat environmental monitoring.

We have also tried to approach these challenges responsibly. Not every proposed feature is an established technology, and not every scientific measurement can directly predict a health outcome. Throughout our development, we have aimed to distinguish established research methods from proposed engineering concepts and features that still require validation.

OUR VISION

Project Proteus represents our effort to look at human spaceflight safety as a connected challenge rather than a collection of unrelated problems. It brings together five areas of research, five dedicated technological approaches and one shared vision: making space exploration safer for the people who undertake it.

We know that there is still a great deal of research, testing and development ahead. Some of our ideas are early-stage concepts that will require extensive validation before they could be used in real missions. But we believe that meaningful innovation begins by understanding the problem, exploring the science and having the courage to develop new approaches.

With Proteus, we hope to contribute to a future where exploring farther into space also means taking better care of the humans who make that exploration possible.
